Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Keep the supplied language.", "input": "The shared studio access list is kept in a blue binder on the shelf beside the entrance, with a matching digital copy in the studio’s operations folder. It records who may enter the room, which days their access is active, and whether they hold a key, use a keypad code, or must be admitted by another member. The list is not a booking calendar, so an access entry does not reserve a worktable or guarantee that the room will be empty. Members check the calendar separately before bringing equipment or inviting a collaborator.

Mara, who coordinates the list, updates the binder on Monday mornings and after any approved change during the week. She writes the effective date beside each new entry and keeps the previous pages in a dated envelope in the locked cabinet. The digital copy has the same names and access details, but it also includes a last-updated field and a note explaining changes. “If the two copies disagree, use the dated paper entry for that day and message me before changing anything,” Mara told the group. The note matters because a paper update may be waiting to sync while the coordinator is away from the computer.

Members submit changes through the studio’s access form rather than writing directly in the binder. A request includes the person’s full name, a contact address, the requested days and hours, an access method, and the date access should begin. The form also asks whether the person needs access for a single project or expects to return regularly. That distinction helps Mara record a clear end date where one is known. If a request does not identify an access method, Mara asks the member to clarify it before entering the change; she does not assume that a new person can use an existing key or code.

1. At the start of each Monday check, compare the digital copy with the most recent dated page in the binder.
2. Confirm that active names, days, end dates, and access methods appear in both places. Mark a difference for follow-up rather than silently changing either copy.
3. Add an approved change with its effective date, then enter the same information in the digital copy and its change note.
4. Put the replaced page in the dated envelope. Do not discard a page simply because every entry on it has expired.
5. Send the person who requested the change a brief confirmation of the recorded dates and method, without including another member’s contact details.

The list uses full names rather than initials because two people in the studio have the same first name. Their contact addresses are kept in the operations folder, not on the binder page that sits near the entrance. The binder shows only the details needed to identify an active entry and use the assigned access method. For a keypad entry, it records that a code is assigned but does not print the code itself. Mara shares a code directly with the person who is authorized to use it and records when the message was sent.

There are two temporary entries this month. Imani has access on Tuesday and Thursday evenings through May 30 while she finishes a set of printed panels. Leo may enter on Saturday mornings through June 8 to repair the studio’s storage carts. Neither entry gives the person permission to bring in an additional guest. If either project runs beyond its listed end date, the member must send a new request before that date; the existing entry does not extend automatically. Mara has written both end dates in the binder and added reminders to the digital change note.

A returned key is logged with the date and the name of the person who received it. If a key is left in the labeled tray instead, Mara notes that it is there but does not mark it returned until she checks the tray herself. The same distinction applies to a code that a member says they have stopped using: the list remains unchanged until Mara verifies that the code has been disabled. “I don’t want a message saying it’s done when it still opens the door,” she said at the last studio meeting. Until verification, the active entry stays visible to the coordinators, and any unresolved question is noted next to it.

When someone reports that an entry is missing, Mara checks the dated paper pages, the digital change note, and the original form. She does not add access based only on a name appearing in a calendar invitation or on a message from someone who is not coordinating the list. If the paperwork supports the request but the effective date is unclear, she contacts the requester and waits for a reply before changing the record. The member can still ask another authorized person to meet them at the entrance, but that arrangement does not become a permanent access entry.

At the end of each month, Mara reviews the upcoming end dates with the members who submitted temporary requests. She records a new date only when a member has asked for an extension and the change is approved through the usual process. Expired names remain on the dated pages for reference, while the current page clearly separates active entries from entries that have ended. The binder stays on the entrance shelf for coordinators to consult, and the operations folder remains available to the small group responsible for maintaining the list.
